amṛta
(‘that which gives इम्मोर्तलित्य्’)
------------------------------------------
The desire to become immortal is most natural to all mortals. Hindu mytho-logy often mentions ‘amṛta,’ the nectar or ambrosia, by drinking which one can become immortal. The story goes that इन्द्र, the king of gods, lost his all to the demons, owing to the curse of the sage दुर्वासस्, whom he had displeased. Lord विष्णु advised him to make up with the demons and with their help, to churn the ocean of milk, out of which अमृत could be got. By drinking it the gods could become immortal and regain their lost sovereignty. अमृत was the last product got out of this churning. Lord विष्णु, in the guise of मोहिनी (the enchantress) successfully deceived the demons and served it to the gods. Inebriated by the new strength and vigour got out of consuming it, the gods routed the demons and regained all they had lost.
See SAMUDRAMATHANA for details.
Garuḍa is said to have brought it from हेअवेन् to give it to कद्रू, his aunt, to release his मोथेर् विनता from her स्लवेर्य्. So also, कृष्ण is believed to have got it for the sage उदङ्क.
The word अमृत is also used in several other senses. For instance: God, मोओन्, लिबेरतिओन्, what is left over after a sacrifice, ड़ोओद् obtained without begging, milk, ghee, an auspicious time of conjunction of certain nakṣatras (stars) with certain week days and so on. The last is also known as ‘amṛtasiddhiyoga.’

Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is a minor Upaniṣad of just 22 verses belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.
It starts with an oft-quoted statement that it is the मिन्द् that is responsible for either bondage or लिबेरतिओन्. When attached to sense objects it leads to bondage; when freed from the same, it leads to लिबेरतिओन्. Hence it should be freed from the bondage of sense-life.
It then delineates the process of meditation by which the मिन्द् bereft of sense-attachments is fixed in the region of the heart on ब्रह्मन्. meditation on ब्रह्मन् can be practised first through the sound of Om, and then directly.
This is followed by an exposition of ब्रह्मन्-आत्मन् with the usual adjectives like niṣkalam (partless), nirañjanam (stainless), aprameyam (immeasurable) and so on. Then the Upaniṣad describes how ब्रह्मन्, the one without a second, appears as many, with the simile of मोओन् and its reflections in water, and, the sky and pots.
It puts forth the theory of two kinds of knowledge, of शब्द-ब्रह्मन् and पर-ब्रह्मन्.
The former is the वेदस् and their branches. A mastering of these can help in leading to the latter, which has to be realized through contemplation. This contemplation is likened to the process of churning milk to get butter, or churning the pieces of अरणि (See ARAṆI.) to get fire. The Upaniṣad ends with a statement of the jñānī, a man of realization, reflecting on his realization of his identity with ब्रह्मन्.
It is interesting to note that there is another Upaniṣad called Brahmabindu Upaniṣad which is almost identical with this Upaniṣad.
See also UPANIṢADS.

amṛtakalaśa
(‘chalice containing ambrosia’)
------------------------------------------
During समुद्रमथन (churning of the milk-ocean) several celestial objects manifested themselves, the last of which was अमृत or ambrosia in a golden vessel (kalaśa) carried by धन्वन्तरि, the celestial physician, considered as an aspect of विष्णु.
The finial of a Hindu temple is shaped like the अमृतकलश, symbolizing इम्मोर्तलित्य्, the state to which the devotee aspires to rise.
See also DHANVANTARI and SAMUDRA-MATHANA.

Amṛtsar
(‘Lake of Nectar’)
------------------------------------------
Amṛtsar or Amritsar is the principal holy city of the Sikhs. It is in Punjab and is also the district headquarters.
The foundation of the city was laid by गुरु Rāmdās (A.

-1581), the fourth गुरु of सिखिस्म्, when he inaugurated the digging of the holy tank ‘Amṛt-sar’ (‘lake of nectar’) on a piece of land purchased from the residents of the neighbouring village of Tuṅg during the time of the previous गुरु, Amardās (A.

-1574). The habitation that grew round the holy lake was initially called ‘Rāmdāspur’ or ‘Chakk Rāmdās’ or ‘Chakk गुरु’.
Guru Arjan (A.

-1606) comple-ted and lined the tank. He also constructed the holy shrine in its middle, “Harimandar’ (now famous as the गोल्देन् तेम्प्ले).
Guru Hargobind (A.

-1644) constructed the Akāl Takht (‘Throne of the Eternal’) near the pool. He also got dug up two more tanks in the town, known as ‘Kaulsar’ and ‘Bibeksar’.
During the eighteenth century, अमृत्सर् witnessed many ups and downs like the Sikh community. It suffered repeatedly, desecration and destruction at the hands of the Muslim rulers of Delhi. Only by the time of Mahārājā Raṇjit Singh (A.

-1830) order and peace were established.
Amṛtsar gradually grew into an important industrial and commercial city.
Amṛtsar has many Sikh shrines associated with the memory of the Gurus, martyrs and heroes. Some of them are: Akāl Buṅga, Gurdwārā Dukh Bhañjanī Berī, Gurdwārā Tharhā Sāhib, Gurdwārā Mañjī Sāhib, Gurdwārā Guruke Mahal, Bābā Aṭal Sāhib, Gurdwārā Rāmsar, Gurdwārā Bibeksar, Gurdwārā Darśanī Diorhī, Gurdwārā Damdamā Sāhib and so on.

Amṛtanāda Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is a small Upaniṣad of 38 verses belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda and classified among the ‘Yoga उपनिषद्स्’ since the subject matter relates to योग.
The Upaniṣad starts with the exhortation to study the scriptures like the वेदस् and their accessories, practise the disciplines taught there, realize the highest ब्रह्मन् and then, give up these scriptures since the purpose of life will have been accomplished.
This is followed by a simile of the chariot in which Om is the chariot and विष्णु (= बुद्धि or intellect) is the charioteer. The aspirant devoted to रुद्र (his own Self) and desirous of attaining ब्रह्मलोक or the abode of ब्रह्मन्, travels in that chariot as far as it goes and then abandons it. The idea is that the aspirant while repeating Om thinks of ‘Rudra’ or his own Self as identified with ब्रह्मन्, through his intellect. When this identity is felt, he abandons the repetition of Om but proceeds to make his meditation deeper, ultimately resulting in direct experience of that oneness.
Then comes the description of ‘Ṣaḍaṅga-योग’ or योग comprising six steps. They are: प्रत्याहार, ध्यान, प्राणायाम, धारणा, तर्क and समाधि. प्रत्याहार (lit., withdrawal of the मिन्द् from the senses) is defined here as thinking of the मिन्द् and the sense-objects as ‘rays emanating from the आत्मन्’ thus neutralizing their effects. ध्यान is meditation on the oneness of आत्मन् with ब्रह्मन्. प्राणायाम is regulation of breath, and through that, regulation of the vital energies or prāṇas. धारणा or fixing the मिन्द् on the objects of meditation, is the earlier stage of ध्यान. तर्क is लोगिच्, not opposed to the teachings of the वेदस्. समाधि is the direct experience of the oneness of the आत्मन् with ब्रह्मन्.
The Upaniṣad gives some details of the process of प्राणायाम, positions and fields of operation of the five prāṇas, certain obstacles to योग like fear, anger and laziness which must be overcome and a few other details connected with yogic practices. It concludes with the statements that if a योगि has mastered the techniques of raising his प्राण through the various plexuses up to the centre of the head, his प्राण will depart, at the time of death, through the ब्रह्मरन्ध्र (aperture in the crown of the head) whatever be the manner of his death, and so, he is never reborn.
See also PRĀṆĀYĀMA and UPANIṢADS.

amṛt
(‘the nectar’)
------------------------------------------
There have been several renaissance movements in हिन्दुइस्म् which have reformed and revitalised it. One of the latest of such movements is the one started by गुरु Nānak (A.

—1538). It is now known as सिखिस्म् and considered as an independent religion.
Guru Gobind Singh (A.

—1708) formed the खाल्सा (lit., ‘personification of the गुरु’) an army of baptised Sikhs. The process of baptism consisted of stirring water in an iron bowl with a double-edged sword, mixing it with sugar and drinking it, as also sprinkling it on the face. Sacred verses from the Guru Granth Sāhib were uttered during the stirring. The water itself was called ‘amṛt’ or nectar. The procedure is followed even now.
See also GURU GOBIND SINGHand SIKHISM.

amṛtatva
(‘immortality’)
------------------------------------------
All living beings are naturally and instinctively struggling for freedom from sorrow and suffering. So also do they seek pleasure and happiness. The उपनिषद्स्, the ancient and basic works of हिन्दुइस्म्, call this state ‘amṛtatva,’ the state of इम्मोर्तलित्य् and bliss. मोक्ष, मुक्ति, निर्वाण and कैवल्य are some of the more common synonyms of the same.
All the Hindu scriptures are unanimous that
amṛtatva is the goal of human life;
the human beings desirous of obtaining it should purify themselves by giving up evil ways of life;
they should take recourse to the śāstras (holy books) and आचार्य (spiritual preceptor), and practise ज्ञान (knowledge) as also भक्ति (devotion) to reach that goal.
Once this goal of अमृतत्व is obtained, there is no return to this life of transmigration. The liberated सोउल् will enjoy eternal bliss.
Details of the path as also the nature of अमृतत्व differ from school to school of religious philosophies.
See also MOKṢA.
